<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Věra Kůrková
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Institute of Computer Science of the Czech Academy of Sciences
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Email: </span><a href="mailto:"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">vera@cs.cas.cz</span></a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">We present a theoretical study of the robustness of parameterized networks to random input perturbations. Specifically, we analyze local robustness at a given network input by quantifying the probability that a small additive random perturbation of the input leads to misclassification. For deep networks with rectified linear units, we derive lower bounds on local robustness in terms of the input dimensionality and the total number of network units.
Our probabilistic robustness estimates are obtained by combining tools from high-dimensional geometry with a characterization of the geometric complexity of the sets of input–output functions of ReLU networks. We show that, for almost all inputs, the lower bounds on local robustness increase rapidly with growing input dimensionality, while decreasing only mildly with the total number of network units, regardless of the layer arrangement. Thus, our results demonstrate the suitability of deep ReLU networks for processing high-dimensional data. Moreover, our probabilistic bounds allow us to identify inputs whose local neighborhoods are likely to contain adversarial patterns.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The reliability of AI systems based on neural networks is crucial for their practical
applicability. In particular, it is desirable that networks maintain their intended functionality even when
exposed to changes or variations in their inputs. The susceptibility of parameterized networks to input
perturbations has been observed in various cases caused either by corruption of data (due to errors or
noise) or by intentionally crafted perturbations. Szegedy et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> initiated
a study of imperceptible perturbations to test images
leading to their misclassification. They called such images <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">adversarial</span> and conjectured that</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">“the set of adversarial negatives
is of extremely low probability, and thus is never (or rarely) observed in the test set,
yet it is dense (much like the rational numbers), and so it is found near virtually every
test case.”</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The discovery of neural network vulnerability led to extensive research on algorithms constructing adversarial patterns that networks misclassify despite their indistinguishability from the training patterns
(see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite> and references therein) and methods of defence against adversarial attacks (see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>).
Theoretical studies of adversarial patterns have been mostly focused on
characterization of the smallest additive perturbations that can change the outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, on comparing the influence of the
worst-case and average perturbations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>]</cite>, and influence of Lipschitz continuity on robustness
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we study the robustness of parameterized neural networks (either trained or randomly initialized) from a probabilistic perspective. We introduce the concept of <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">local robustness</span> at an input <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to a precision parameter <math id="S1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>
defined as the probability that the network misclassifies an input obtained by applying an additive random perturbation of magnitude <math id="S1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. Such perturbed images remain within a Euclidean distance <math id="S1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> from the original. For sufficiently small values of <math id="S1.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, perturbed images are likely to be indistinguishable to the human eye from the training image.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Neural networks typically process data represented as high-dimensional vectors.
Geometry of high-dimensional spaces exhibits some counterintuitive properties, called the “blessing
of dimensionality” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, which make some tasks easier or predictable. These benefits of high-dimension are based on the “concentration of measure phenomenon” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, which implies, e.g., the concentration of the volume and the surface
of high-dimensional spheres <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, the reduction of dimensionality by random projections <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, and the exponential growth of the quasi-orthogonal dimension <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>.
High-dimensional geometry also affects functionality and accuracy of neural networks (see e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we investigate how input dimensionality influences the local robustness of parameterized deep ReLU networks. We derive probabilistic lower bounds on their local robustness in terms of the input dimension and the total number of units. Our lower bounds on local robustness, for almost all inputs in <math id="S1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, grow rapidly with increasing input dimensionality <math id="S1.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, while exhibiting only a mild decrease with respect to the total number of units, independently of how these units are distributed across layers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Our theoretical analysis is based on the characterization of the geometric complexity of the sets of input–output functions of deep ReLU networks, exploiting their piecewise-linear, plane-wave structure. By combining this structural characterization with properties of high-dimensional spheres, we derive probabilistic estimates of local robustness. Our estimates imply that, in deep ReLU networks, adversarial examples are unlikely to be found under random testing in high dimensions. They also allow us to identify inputs whose local neighborhoods are likely to contain adversarial patterns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Preliminaries ‣ Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> introduces the necessary background, notation, and preliminary concepts. Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Probabilistic approach to robustness ‣ Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> develops a probabilistic framework for analyzing robustness to misclassification caused by random additive perturbations. Within this framework, we first illustrate the fundamental role of data dimensionality using the example of classification by a single Heaviside perceptron, and then extend the probabilistic misclassification bounds to shallow perceptron networks. Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Robustness of deep ReLU networks ‣ Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> includes structural analysis of sets of input-output functions of deep ReLU networks and exploits it to derive our main results on their robustness. Finally, Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Conclusion ‣ Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> concludes with a summary and discussion of the consequences of our results for the hypothesis of Szegedy et. al <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> that motivated our work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Preliminaries</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Feedforward networks</span> compute parameterized families of input-output (I/O) functions
determined by directed acyclic graphs, where nodes represent computational units and edges represent connections between them.
In <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">multilayer networks</span>, units are arranged in layers, inputs in <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> are viewed as the layer <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>,
layers <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=1,\dots,L-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=1,\dots,L-1</annotation></semantics></math> are called <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hidden layers</span>, and the number of layers <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> is called
the <span id="S2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">network depth</span>. In this paper, we focus on networks where <span id="S2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">connections to any layer
are only from the preceding layer</span>, and where the <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">-th layer contains only one output unit</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Typical computational units apply a fixed <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">activation function</span> <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi:{\mathbb{R}}\to{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> to <span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">affine
functions with varying parameters</span>. The units compute functions of the form</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\psi(v\cdot.+b):{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">.</mo><mo lspace="0em">+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo rspace="0.278em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.278em">:</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi(v\cdot.+b):{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to{\mathbb{R}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> is called a <span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">weight vector</span>, <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\in{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\in{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math> a <span id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bias</span>, and</p>
<table id="S2.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\cdot x=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_{i}x_{i}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>d</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\cdot x=\sum_{i=1}^{d}v_{i}x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">denotes the <span id="S2.p3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scalar product</span>.
These units have been called <span id="S2.p3.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">perceptrons</span> because their form was inspired by a naive
model of a neuron with hard
(Heaviside, signum) or soft (hyperbolic tangent, logistic sigmoid) threshold functions
as activations. Currently, the most popular activation function is the rectified linear function
(ReLU) function due to its suitability for gradient-based learning.
We denote by <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta:{\mathbb{R}}\to\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>ℝ</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta:{\mathbb{R}}\to\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>
the  <span id="S2.p3.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Heaviside function</span></p>

<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">and for <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\in{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\in{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math>, by</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

</div>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">the <span id="S2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">hyperplane</span> determined by <math id="S2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">For our study, it is essential that functions computed by perceptrons with any activation function have the form of <span id="S2.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">plane waves</span>. They are constant on hyperplanes
parallel to <math id="S2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math>. We denote</p>
<table id="S2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}^{-}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,|\,v\cdot x+b\leq 0\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.170em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}^{-}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,|\,v\cdot x+b\leq 0\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<table id="S2.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}^{+}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,|\,v\cdot x+b&gt;0\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.170em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}^{+}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,|\,v\cdot x+b&gt;0\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">the two <span id="S2.p7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">half-spaces</span> separated by <math id="S2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math>. Note that we define the half-spaces
in such a way that the hyperplane <math id="S2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math> is contained in the half-space <math id="S2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{-}_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{-}_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math> , so <math id="S2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{-}_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{-}_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math> is closed and <math id="S2.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H^{+}_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H^{+}_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math> is open. The reason is that the function <math id="S2.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rho" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ρ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rho</annotation></semantics></math> is equal to zero on the half-line <math id="S2.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\infty,0]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\infty,0]</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus <math id="S2.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{d}=H^{+}_{v,b}\cup H^{-}_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>∪</mo><msubsup><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo></msubsup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{d}=H^{+}_{v,b}\cup H^{-}_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p">For <math id="S2.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, we denote by <math id="S2.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{H_{v,b}}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{H_{v,b}}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> the
<span id="S2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">orthogonal
projection</span> of <math id="S2.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> onto <math id="S2.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math> and
for <math id="S2.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
<table id="S2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<p id="S2.p8.2" class="ltx_p">the <span id="S2.p8.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Euclidean distance</span>
of <math id="S2.p8.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S2.p8.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, by <math id="S2.p8.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{r}^{d-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{r}^{d-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> the <span id="S2.p8.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">sphere</span> in <math id="S2.p8.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> of radius <math id="S2.p8.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> centered at <math id="S2.p8.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>,
and by <math id="S2.p8.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{d-1}:=S_{1}^{d-1}(0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{d-1}:=S_{1}^{d-1}(0)</annotation></semantics></math> the <span id="S2.p8.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unit
sphere</span> centered at <math id="S2.p8.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">We denote by</p>

</div>
<div id="S2.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p10.1" class="ltx_p">the <span id="S2.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">parameterized <math id="S2.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>-layer network</span>, where each of the layers <math id="S2.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l=1,\dots,L-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l=1,\dots,L-1</annotation></semantics></math>
contains <math id="S2.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> perceptrons
with ReLU activations and parameters <math id="S2.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{l,j},b_{l,j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{l,j},b_{l,j}</annotation></semantics></math>, and the layer <math id="S2.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> contains one
Heaviside perceptron computing <math id="S2.p10.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta(v_{L}\cdot y_{L-1}+b_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>L</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta(v_{L}\cdot y_{L-1}+b_{L})</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S2.p10.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y_{L-1}=(y_{L-1,1},\dots,y_{L-1,n_{L-1}})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{L-1}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y_{L-1}=(y_{L-1,1},\dots,y_{L-1,n_{L-1}})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n_{L-1}}</annotation></semantics></math>
is the vector of outputs of
<math id="S2.p10.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{L-1}</annotation></semantics></math> units in the <math id="S2.p10.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(L-1)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(L-1)</annotation></semantics></math>-st layer, and by</p>
<table id="S2.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<p id="S2.p10.2" class="ltx_p">the <span id="S2.p10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">input-output (I/O) function</span> of the network <math id="S2.p10.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{N}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>

</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Probabilistic approach to robustness</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a parameterized network <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{N}}</annotation></semantics></math> (with parameters obtained by training or set randomly) that computes
an I/O function <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{{\mathcal{N}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{{\mathcal{N}}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and for an input <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, we study the local robustness of <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{N}}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> in probabilistic terms.
We assume that <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> is modified by an additive random perturbation <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> of a given size <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, formally, by <math id="S3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> drawn from the sphere <math id="S3.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{r}^{d-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{r}^{d-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> according to the uniform probability <math id="S3.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\rm P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\rm P}</annotation></semantics></math>. The Euclidean distance between <math id="S3.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x+\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x+\xi</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S3.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, and therefore for small <math id="S3.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math>, in the case of images, these two inputs might be indistinguishable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We measure robustness of a parameterized network <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{N}}</annotation></semantics></math> by the probability that
<math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{{\mathcal{N}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{{\mathcal{N}}}</annotation></semantics></math> maps <math id="S3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x+\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ξ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x+\xi</annotation></semantics></math> to the same class as <math id="S3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>. Formally, we define the
<span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">local robustness of <math id="S3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\mathcal{N}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{N}}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math> to perturbations of the size <math id="S3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math></span> as</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathcal{R}}(f_{{\mathcal{N}}},x,r):={\rm P}[\,f_{{\mathcal{N}}}(x+\xi)=f_{{\mathcal{N}}}(x)\,]." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo rspace="0.170em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{R}}(f_{{\mathcal{N}}},x,r):={\rm P}[\,f_{{\mathcal{N}}}(x+\xi)=f_{{\mathcal{N}}}(x)\,].</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To gain insight into the robustness of networks computing plane waves,
we begin with the simplest case: a single Heaviside perceptron.
Let</p>
<table id="S3.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x):=\vartheta(v\cdot x+b)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x):=\vartheta(v\cdot x+b)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p4.2" class="ltx_p">be the I/O
function of a parameterized
perceptron with parameters <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b\in{\mathbb{R}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b\in{\mathbb{R}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S3.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math> be the
domain of its inputs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Our probabilistic lower bound on its robustness relies on a counterintuitive geometric phenomenon in high dimensions: the fraction of the <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>-dimensional sphere occupied by a polar cap of fixed angular radius decreases exponentially fast with
<math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> (see Fig. 1).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S3.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S3.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18674v1/capsof.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:197/188;" width="197" height="188"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Spherical polar cap.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 3.1</span></span><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to\{0,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\to\{0,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>, defined as <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(x)=\vartheta(v\cdot x+b)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>ϑ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x)=\vartheta(v\cdot x+b)</annotation></semantics></math>, be an I/O function
of a perceptron with the Heaviside activation <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\vartheta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϑ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\vartheta</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> be a size of a perturbation. Then for every
<math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(x)=\|p(x)-x\|_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(x)=\|p(x)-x\|_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x)</annotation></semantics></math> is the orthogonal projection of <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>
on the hyperplane <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H_{v,b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H_{v,b}</annotation></semantics></math>,and <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\xi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ξ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\xi</annotation></semantics></math> drawn uniformly randomly from <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{r}^{d-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{r}^{d-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>, we have:
<br class="ltx_break">(i) for <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0&lt;a(x)\leq r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>r</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0&lt;a(x)\leq r</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathcal{R}}(f,x,r):={\rm P}[f(x)=f(x+\xi)]&gt;1-e^{-\frac{a(x)^{2}d}{2r^{2}}};" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup><mo>;</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{R}}(f,x,r):={\rm P}[f(x)=f(x+\xi)]&gt;1-e^{-\frac{a(x)^{2}d}{2r^{2}}};</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(ii) for <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a(x)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a(x)=0</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>
<table id="S3.Ex12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex12.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\mathcal{R}}(f,x,r):={\rm P}[(f(x)=f(x+\xi)]=1/2;" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℛ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>ξ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>;</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\mathcal{R}}(f,x,r):={\rm P}[(f(x)=f(x+\xi)]=1/2;</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(iii) for <math id="S3.Thmtheorem1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r&lt;a(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r&lt;a(x)</annotation></semantics></math>,</span></p>

<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proof. </span> For <math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)</annotation></semantics></math>, let</p>
<table id="S3.Ex14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(y,\alpha):=\{z\in S^{d-1}\,|\,|z\cdot y|\geq\arccos\alpha\}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.170em">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mi>arccos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(y,\alpha):=\{z\in S^{d-1}\,|\,|z\cdot y|\geq\arccos\alpha\}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">denotes the <span id="S3.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">spherical polar cap</span> formed by the vectors from the sphere
<math id="S3.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> with the angular distance to <math id="S3.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> at most <math id="S3.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (see Fig. 1).
Let <math id="S3.p6.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> denote the
normalized Lebesgue measure on <math id="S3.p6.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, then for every <math id="S3.p6.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math> and every
<math id="S3.p6.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)</annotation></semantics></math>, the polar cap <math id="S3.p6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C(y,\alpha)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C(y,\alpha)</annotation></semantics></math> satisfies</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu(C(y,\alpha))\leq e^{-\frac{(\cos\alpha)^{2}\,d}{2}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>μ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>α</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu(C(y,\alpha))\leq e^{-\frac{(\cos\alpha)^{2}\,d}{2}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">(see, e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, Lemma 2.2., p.11]</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Rescaling and translating
<math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{r}^{d-1}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{r}^{d-1}(x)</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{d-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{d-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, we obtain from (<a href="#S3.E3" title="In 3 Probabilistic approach to robustness ‣ Robustness of Deep ReLU Networks to Misclassification of High-Dimensional Data" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) for every <math id="S3.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in S^{d-1}_{r}(x)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in S^{d-1}_{r}(x)</annotation></semantics></math>,</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">
